value_chain_position: Major vertically-integrated copper producer (mine through smelter) - sells copper concentrate, cathode, and byproduct gold/moly; not a diversified multi-commodity major.
cost_curve_verified: Proxy and company agree that this is NOT a low-cost producer: the deterministic proxy puts Freeport's 34.8% trailing cash operating margin in the highest-cost quartile of its copper cohort (12th percentile of eight names), and the company's own 2027 target for its United States mines is $2.50 a pound, which management called challenging; the flattering $1.90-a-pound 2026 unit cost guide (cut from $1.95 in July 2026, versus $1.97 actually delivered in the June 2026 quarter) is net of by-product credits struck at $4,000-an-ounce gold and excludes $284 million of idle-facility costs during the Grasberg ramp, so the headline understates the true cost position rather than contradicting the proxy.
gm_trajectory: Gross margin is recovering off a disaster trough but on falling revenue: 34.1% in the June 2025 quarter, down to 18.1% in the December 2025 quarter after the Grasberg mudflow, back to 26.5% and then 31.1% in the March and June 2026 quarters - yet June 2026 revenue of $7.03 billion was 7.3% BELOW the year-earlier $7.58 billion even though the realised copper price rose from roughly $4.50 to $6.17 a pound, meaning a 37% better price did not offset the lost volume.
bull_thesis: The bull case is that investors are buying a 25-year reserve life in the one metal the world is short of, from a management team that does what it says, at the exact moment its largest asset comes back on line. Three things have to be true, and two of them already are. First, the volumes. Consolidated copper sales go from 3.1 billion pounds in 2026 to 3.8 billion in 2027 and 4.1 billion in 2028 - a 32% step-up over two years - as the Grasberg Block Cave in Indonesia recovers from the September 2025 mudflow. The recovery is measurable, not promised: daily production doubled from 34,000 tonnes in April 2026 to 69,000 in June, and management has committed to roughly 65% of full capacity in the second half of 2026, 80% by mid-2027 and near-full by the end of 2027. Second, the price. Copper traded at a record $6.65 a pound on the COMEX exchange on 4 August 2026, against a 200-day average of $5.81 and a 2025 average of $4.51; Freeport realised $6.17 a pound in the June 2026 quarter. On the company's own published sensitivity, every ten cents a pound is worth roughly $390 million of cash operating profit, and its own slides show average annual cash operating profit of roughly $18 billion for 2027-2028 at $6.00-a-pound copper, rising to roughly $24 billion at $7.00. Against trailing cash operating profit of $9.0 billion, that is a doubling from a base that is already funding a dividend and a buyback. Third, the structural United States position, which is the part the market prices least well. Freeport produces more than 70% of America's refined copper and already owns the smelting, refining and concentrate-leach capacity that every new domestic project lacks - Quirk, April 2025: 'we already have the smelter. We already have the tank house capacity.' Since April 2026 semi-finished copper carries a 50% national-security tariff, and the COMEX-versus-London premium has been running near 19 cents a pound, roughly eight times its twenty-year average. On roughly a billion pounds of United States output that is a real margin nobody else can capture. Layered on top are four genuinely unpriced options: the February 2026 memorandum with the Indonesian government extending operating rights for the life of the resource (which pushes Grasberg's value past the 2041 cliff); El Abra in Chile, whose environmental statement was filed in March 2026 and which carries roughly 17.5 billion pounds of copper attached to a potential mill; the Bagdad brownfield expansion in Arizona, de-risked by an autonomous truck conversion and awaiting a decision; and the leach programme, which turns 40 billion pounds of waste stockpile into what Quirk called 'essentially a new mine in the United States' at a target of 800 million pounds a year. The financial condition supports all of it without a share sale: net debt of $6.28 billion including leases is 0.7 times trailing cash operating profit, and $6.3 billion has gone back to shareholders since June 2021. The conditions that must hold are simple to state: copper must stay above roughly $5.50 a pound, the Grasberg ramp must not slip again, and the amended Indonesian mining licence must actually be issued.
bear_thesis: The bear case is not that Freeport is a bad company. It is that at $67.50 a share you are buying a high-cost, unhedged, half-owned bet on record copper prices, and you are paying a full price for it. Start with what you actually own. Consolidated cash operating profit is not shareholders' cash operating profit: the Indonesian government owns 51.24% of the Grasberg subsidiary, Sumitomo owns 28% of Morenci and minorities hold 46% of Cerro Verde in Peru. In the June 2026 quarter, $402 million of $1.386 billion of profit from continuing operations - 29% - went to those partners, and across the trailing year the leakage was about 36%. On a like-for-like basis, adding the $12.1 billion carrying value of those minority interests to the $97.4 billion market value and $6.28 billion of net debt puts the true claim on this business at roughly $115 billion, or 12.8 times trailing cash operating profit, against 8.6 times for BHP, 7.4 times for Teck and 7.2 times for Rio Tinto on today's equally strong commodity prices. Strip the minorities out of the forward numbers and at $67.50 the shares already discount roughly nine to ten times the 2027-2028 cash operating profit that Freeport itself projects at $6.00-a-pound copper. There is no discount here to close. Second, the torque cuts both ways and the bear case must price it. Freeport's measured sensitivity to copper is 0.91 - it moves nearly one-for-one with the metal - and the metal is at an all-time high. Using the company's own sensitivity of about $390 million of cash operating profit per ten cents a pound, a 10% fall in copper from $6.65 to $5.99 removes about $2.6 billion, roughly 13% of the roughly $19.6 billion the business would earn at spot. A return to the 2024-2025 average of about $4.50 removes about $8.6 billion - close to half. That is not a hypothetical: copper averaged $4.15 a pound in 2024 and $4.51 in 2025, and Freeport's own shares traded at $35.15 within the last twelve months. Third, the cost position is worse than the headline. The $1.90-a-pound guide is net of by-product credits struck at $4,000-an-ounce gold; on a gross basis the company's own 2027 target for its United States mines is $2.50 a pound, described by management as challenging given energy and acid costs. The proxy cohort ranking agrees, placing Freeport's 34.8% cash operating margin in the highest-cost quartile - roughly half of Southern Copper's 63%. A high-cost producer at a record price is the most dangerous combination in mining: the margin is entirely price, not position. Fourth, cash generation today is far thinner than the screen suggests. The trailing 'free cash flow' figure of $5.92 billion is actually operating cash flow - the data feed records capital spending as zero. Freeport spent $2.1 billion in the first half of 2026 and guides to $4.3 billion for 2026 and $4.8 billion for 2027. Real trailing free cash flow is closer to $1.7 billion, a yield of about 1.8%, and first-half 2026 free cash flow was roughly $1.4 billion. The full-year operating cash flow guide of $8.3 billion requires $4.8 billion in the second half - a hockey stick that needs both the ramp and the record price to hold simultaneously. Fifth, the sector's oldest error is visible in its early stage: capital spending is rising into the price peak, $4.3 billion to $4.8 billion, of which $1.6 billion in 2026 is explicitly discretionary, while the buyback bought 1.7 million shares near $64.71 in the June 2026 quarter after buying at an average of $36.41 in the first half of 2025. Sixth, single-asset risk is proven, not theoretical: the September 2025 mudflow killed seven workers, triggered force majeure and cost roughly a year of production from an asset carrying close to half the company's earning power; the April 2026 call revealed the ramp was gated on ore chutes that could not handle wet material, and the PB1 South restart is still 'middle of next year'. Seventh, the Indonesian extension is a memorandum, not a licence - the amended special mining permit has not been issued and no date has been published - and the price of the deal is a further 12% of the subsidiary transferred at no cost in 2041, cutting Freeport to roughly 37%. Eighth, the tariff premium is policy, not physics: refined copper was exempted from the Section 232 tariff, and the premium collapsed once before. Finally, the people who know the ramp schedule best are not buying: zero open-market purchases against twelve sales totalling 632,274 shares. What would confirm the bear case: copper closing back below its 200-day average near $5.81; the third-quarter 2026 report in late October failing to show the promised 65%-of-capacity rate; or 2027 capital spending guided above $4.8 billion.
sop_bull: $90 a share. Favourable case assumes copper sustains $7.50 a pound with gold at $4,000 and molybdenum at $30, the Grasberg ramp lands on the published schedule, the leach programme reaches its 800-million-pound path and the amended Indonesian licence is issued. Consolidated cash operating profit reaches roughly $24 billion for 2027-2028 (the company's own slide ladder shows roughly $24 billion at $7.00 copper), including about $1 billion of leach uplift. Deduct the outside partners' share - the Indonesian government's 51.24% of Grasberg, Sumitomo's 28% of Morenci, the 46% Cerro Verde minority - leaving roughly $14.4 billion attributable to Freeport shareholders. At 8.5 times, a modest premium to the 7.2-8.6 times BHP, Rio Tinto and Teck command today, that is about $122 billion of enterprise value; less roughly $4.6 billion of Freeport's share of net debt gives about $118 billion of equity, or $81.60 a share on 1,443 million shares. Add roughly $8 a share for the growth options that a two-year earnings multiple does not capture (El Abra, Bagdad and Lone Star sulphides, and Grasberg's post-2041 tail at the reduced 37% interest). Total: $90.
sop_bear: $33 a share. Adverse case assumes the copper cycle turns against the chain: the metal reverts to $4.50 a pound (above the 2024 low of $3.67 and close to the $4.15 and $4.51 averages of 2024 and 2025), gold falls to $3,500 an ounce so the by-product credit that flatters unit costs shrinks, the Grasberg ramp slips a further year on a repeat of the wet-ore handling problem, and United States unit costs settle at $2.70 a pound rather than the $2.50 target. Consolidated cash operating profit falls to roughly $9.5 billion - the company's own sensitivity of about $390 million per ten cents a pound implies a fall of about $8.6 billion from spot-price levels, close to half the business. Deduct the outside partners' share and roughly $5.7 billion is attributable to Freeport shareholders. Miners re-rate upward on trough earnings, so apply 9.0 times rather than a cycle-peak multiple: about $51 billion of enterprise value. Net debt rises to roughly $7.6 billion as $4.8 billion of 2027 capital spending outruns cash generation, leaving about $44 billion of equity, or $30.30 a share. Growth options are written down to a residual $3 billion, or about $2.10 a share. Total: $33 - which is close to, and slightly below, the $35.15 the shares actually traded at within the last twelve months when copper was near $5.00 and Grasberg was shut.
sop_fair_value: $60 a share (base case; defensible band $56 to $63 depending on whether the attributable multiple is 7.0 or 8.0 times).
sop_breakdown: Built from the 2027-2028 run-rate at $6.20-a-pound copper (deliberately between the 200-day average of $5.81 and the record $6.65 spot - a miner should never be underwritten at record spot), $4,000-an-ounce gold and $30-a-pound molybdenum, which produces roughly $17.8 billion of CONSOLIDATED cash operating profit. Parts, valued on Freeport's economic share of each: Indonesia (Grasberg Block Cave, Kucing Liar, Deep Mill Level Zone plus the new smelter and precious-metals refinery) contributes roughly $8.5 billion of consolidated cash operating profit at full rate but Freeport owns only 48.76%, so roughly $4.1 billion attributable, valued at 5.5 times for the 51% government ownership, the unissued mining licence and the demonstrated single-asset operating risk: about $23 billion. North America (Morenci at 72%, Bagdad, Safford/Lone Star, Sierrita, the Miami smelter and the leach programme) contributes roughly $5.5 billion consolidated and about $4.7 billion attributable, valued at 8.5 times for tariff-protected refined copper, no expropriation risk and brownfield growth: about $40 billion. South America (Cerro Verde at 53.56%, El Abra at 51%) contributes roughly $3.4 billion consolidated and about $1.8 billion attributable at 6.0 times: about $11 billion. Atlantic Copper in Spain and other operations add about $1 billion. Corporate costs subtract about $5 billion. That gives roughly $70 billion of enterprise value attributable to Freeport shareholders on about $10.7 billion of attributable cash operating profit - a blended 7.5 times. Subtract Freeport's share of net debt, roughly $4.6 billion (consolidated net debt including leases is $6.28 billion at 30 June 2026, of which $3.2 billion sits at the Indonesian downstream facility and is only 48.76% Freeport's), leaving about $76 billion of equity or $52.50 a share on 1,443 million shares. Add roughly $10 billion of risked growth options that a two-year earnings multiple cannot capture - El Abra (about $2 billion), Bagdad and Lone Star sulphides (about $2.5 billion), the leach programme beyond the 300-million-pound milestone (about $2.5 billion) and Grasberg's post-2041 tail at the reduced roughly 37% interest (about $3 billion) - or about $6.90 a share. Base fair value: $60. The single most important line in this build is the minority deduction: consolidated cash operating profit overstates what shareholders own by 36% to 40%, and the market's habit of quoting Freeport on consolidated enterprise value to cash operating profit hides that.
risk_reward: Poor for a fresh entry today. At $67.50 the shares sit roughly 12% ABOVE the $60 base-case sum-of-the-parts value, so there is no upside to fair value to collect - a buyer today is already paying for part of the $90 favourable case. The adverse case sits at $33, and that level is credible rather than theoretical: the shares traded at $35.15 within the last twelve months, with copper near $5.00 and Grasberg shut. The asymmetry is therefore negative at this price. It turns favourable below roughly $50, which would restore a genuine margin of safety to the base case; that level has historically appeared whenever copper retraces toward its 200-day average, currently $5.81 a pound, and the shares' own 200-day average is $57.10.
catalyst_status_note: The load-bearing event is the extension of operating rights at Grasberg in Indonesia. On 18 February 2026 Freeport announced a memorandum of understanding with the Indonesian government for a life-of-resource extension for its Indonesian subsidiary, under which Freeport keeps 48.76% through 2041 and transfers a further 12% at no cost in 2041, falling to roughly 37% from 2042. As of 4 August 2026 that remains a memorandum: the amended special mining business licence that gives it legal effect has not been issued, and no completion date has been published. It is therefore a soft, non-binding commitment with no contractual payout and no fixed date. This status is recorded for the file only and did not drive the verdict - dated-event asymmetry belongs to a different book. The other events in the file are not catalysts in this sense: the Grasberg restart is an operating ramp with a published schedule (roughly 65% of capacity in the second half of 2026, 80% by mid-2027, near-full by end-2027), and the third-quarter 2026 results, due around late October 2026, are a scheduled report rather than a binding event.
peer_comps_note: Against the assigned true competitors, on trailing enterprise value to cash operating profit as of 4 August 2026: Southern Copper 16.7 times, BHP 8.6 times, Teck 7.4 times, Rio Tinto 7.2 times, Freeport 11.5 times on the conventional measure. That comparison flatters Freeport, because the conventional measure excludes the $12.1 billion carrying value of the minority interests while including all of their cash operating profit; put on a consistent basis, the full claim on Freeport's business is about $115 billion, or 12.8 times trailing - the most expensive in the group except Southern Copper. Southern Copper is a poor anchor in any case: it earns a 63% cash operating margin against Freeport's 34.8%, holds a lower-cost asset base and a controlled share register, and has structurally traded at a premium for years. The honest read from this comp set is that the diversified majors trade at 7 to 8.6 times trailing cash operating profit at today's strong commodity prices, and Freeport at $67.50 is asking roughly nine to ten times its 2027-2028 attributable earnings at $6.00-a-pound copper. The multiple, not the asset, is the problem.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is not about copper and not about Freeport's quality - it is about arithmetic. The Street's published targets cluster at $70 to $82 (consensus $72.41, median $73.00, high $82.00, low $58.50), and the six targets set in the last month average $76.17 against a share price of $61 to $63 at the time they were written. Those targets are overwhelmingly built by applying a multiple to CONSOLIDATED cash operating profit or to consensus earnings per share. Two specific assumptions inside that approach are wrong. First, roughly 36% to 40% of Freeport's consolidated cash operating profit does not belong to Freeport shareholders. The Indonesian government owns 51.24% of the Grasberg subsidiary, Sumitomo 28% of Morenci and minorities 46% of Cerro Verde. In the June 2026 quarter alone, $402 million of $1.386 billion of profit from continuing operations - 29% - was attributed away; across the trailing year the leakage was about 36%. A consolidated multiple that ignores the $12.1 billion of minority interests on the balance sheet is not comparing like with like against BHP or Rio Tinto, whose minorities are trivial. Correct for it and the peer discount the Street believes it is buying disappears. Second, the consensus forward earnings growth of about 36% requires the Grasberg ramp and record copper to hold at the same time - and those two are negatively related. Grasberg's return of 700 million-plus pounds of annual copper is itself a meaningful part of the 2027 supply that the market's own deficit forecasts assume away; management's slide deck quotes analysts projecting 2026 as 'tightly balanced', with some forecasting small surpluses, not a deficit. The Street is underwriting a supply-driven price and a supply-driven volume recovery from the same barrel. Third, and more subtly, the market is reading the $1.90-a-pound unit cost guide as evidence of a low-cost producer. It is not: that figure is net of by-product credits struck at $4,000-an-ounce gold, and Freeport's own 2027 target for its United States mines is $2.50 a pound, which management called challenging. On the cohort measure, Freeport's 34.8% cash operating margin sits in the highest-cost quartile of eight copper names. Where we AGREE with the market: the asset base is exceptional, the balance sheet is genuinely conservative at 0.7 times net debt to cash operating profit, management delivers what it guides, and the United States refining position is a durable and under-appreciated advantage. Our disagreement is entirely about price.
valley_of_death: The risky window is the next three to nine months, and it has five distinct pressure points. First, the ramp itself. Grasberg is only promised at roughly 65% of full capacity across the second half of 2026, and the April 2026 call revealed the constraint was mechanical - ore chutes that could not handle the wet-to-dry ore ratio in production blocks two and three. Management believes 'this is the big one' and that solving it unlocks the rest, but the PB1 South block is still only scheduled to restart 'middle of next year' and the PB1C block has no firm plan at all. Any repeat pushes the 3.8 billion pounds guided for 2027. Second, the cash-flow shape. Full-year 2026 operating cash flow is guided at $8.3 billion, of which only $3.5 billion arrived in the first half - the second half needs $4.8 billion, which requires both the ramp and record prices simultaneously. Against that, capital spending is $4.3 billion in 2026 rising to $4.8 billion in 2027. First-half 2026 free cash flow was roughly $1.4 billion. If copper retraces while capital spending steps up, free cash flow compresses toward zero in a hurry - and the screener's headline free-cash-flow figure of $5.92 billion is not a cushion, because it is actually operating cash flow with capital spending recorded as zero; the real trailing figure is closer to $1.7 billion. Third, the headline cost number gets worse before it gets better in an honest accounting sense. Freeport excluded $284 million of idle-facility costs from its June 2026 unit cash cost, and the excluded pool at Grasberg rose from $900 million to $1.3 billion between January and April 2026. Those are real cash costs; they simply do not appear in the reported cost per pound until the ramp completes. Fourth, the price itself. Copper set a record $6.65 a pound on 4 August 2026, and a meaningful part of the United States price is a tariff artefact: semi-finished copper carries a 50% national-security tariff since April 2026, but refined copper was exempted, and the COMEX-versus-London premium has already collapsed once on an exemption announcement. It currently runs near 19 cents a pound, about eight times its long-run average. That premium is a policy decision, and policy can be revised without notice. Fifth, the Indonesian licence. The February 2026 memorandum has not become an amended mining permit, and Indonesia has a long history of using permit renewals as leverage - the 7.5% export duty of 2025 being the most recent example. There is no debt wall (net debt is 0.7 times cash operating profit and there is no near-term maturity concern) and no cash-burn risk. The danger here is not solvency. It is that a stock priced above its base-case value meets a quarter in which the ramp disappoints, the tariff premium narrows, or copper simply mean-reverts toward its 200-day average of $5.81.
positioning_washout: There is no forced-selling setup here, and that is part of the problem - this is a crowded, well-owned momentum name, not a washed-out one. The shares sit roughly 87% of the way up their twelve-month range of $35.15 to $72.28, about 18% above their 200-day average of $57.10, and rose 6.1% on 4 August alone alongside a record copper price. Options-implied volatility was flagged as surging in late July 2026. The shareholder register is institutional and index-heavy rather than yield-driven, so there is no dividend-cut mechanism that would force liquidation: the quarterly dividend of $0.15 a share (half base, half variable) yields under 1% and is covered many times over, and management's stated policy of returning about 50% of excess cash flow explicitly excludes discretionary project spending, so the dividend is not the pressure valve. What the filings actually show is quiet distribution rather than accumulation: Amundi cut its holding 24.8% and Bank of Nova Scotia 16.6% in the first quarter of 2026, against smaller additions elsewhere, and insiders sold 632,274 shares across twelve open-market transactions with no purchases at all. The mechanical flow risk runs the other way. Because Freeport's sensitivity to copper is 0.91 and it is the largest liquid copper pure-play available to United States investors, it is the default vehicle for macro and exchange-traded-fund flow into the copper theme. That flow is momentum-following and it reverses fast. A move in copper back toward $5.50 would take the systematic bid out at the same moment the fundamental bid weakens - the classic mechanism by which a high-beta miner gives back a quarter of its value in weeks. The washout that would create an entry has not happened; it is the thing to wait for.
forcing_function: Three dated or near-dated events will settle this. The first and most important is the third-quarter 2026 results, expected around late October 2026 (the scan puts the next report about 80 days out). That is the first full quarter that must actually print the promised roughly 65%-of-capacity Grasberg rate and the guided 750 million pounds of copper sales; it is also the first quarter in which the second-half operating cash flow hockey stick of $4.8 billion has to start appearing. A clean print with $2.5 billion-plus of operating cash flow confirms the ramp; a miss on volumes re-opens the whole 2027 volume bridge. The second is the issuance of the amended special mining business licence in Indonesia, which converts the 18 February 2026 memorandum into an enforceable life-of-resource extension. No date has been published, which is precisely why it is not yet a valuation event - but issuance would justify a materially lower risk discount on the roughly $23 billion of attributable Indonesian value in our sum-of-the-parts, which we currently capitalise at only 5.5 times. The third is the Bagdad expansion decision, which management said in April 2026 it was 'completing our work to be in a position to potentially greenlight... later this year'. A go-decision converts an option into a capital commitment and will tell you whether the 2027 capital spending guide of $4.8 billion is a ceiling or a floor. For our purposes the more useful forcing function is price, not event: a retracement in copper toward its 200-day average of $5.81 a pound would very likely take the shares toward $50, at which point the base-case value of $60 offers a real margin of safety.
moderator_conclusion: This is a genuinely good business at a price that has run past it, and the honest call is to wait rather than to pass or to chase. Take the good news first, because it is real. Freeport owns roughly 86.8 billion pounds of proven and probable copper reserves against consolidated sales of 3.1 billion pounds this year - about a 25-year life in the one metal whose demand story nobody seriously disputes. Its balance sheet is conservative by the standards of an industry famous for wrecking itself at the top: net debt of $6.28 billion including leases, 0.7 times trailing cash operating profit, no equity issuance, no dilution. Management's record on the things it controls is strong - the Indonesian smelter was delivered a month early after a fire, the export duty went to zero in 2026 exactly as promised a year in advance, 2025 unit costs landed within 3% of the original guide despite a disaster that removed a tenth of the year's volume, and cost guidance was CUT from $1.95 to $1.90 a pound in July 2026. Management even corrects analysts for being too bearish, using the right minority-interest arithmetic. The forensic file is clean. Now the three reasons not to buy it here. First, contracting and price exposure: Freeport does not hedge. Nothing across five earnings calls describes fixed-price offtake, forward sales or collars - sales are made at benchmark-linked prices with provisional pricing marks to its own smelters, Japanese and Korean smelters, and Swiss-domiciled traders. Shareholders take the entire price move in both directions, and the metal is at an all-time high of $6.65 a pound against a 200-day average of $5.81 and 2024-2025 averages of $4.15 and $4.51. Torque is symmetric: on the company's own sensitivity of about $390 million of cash operating profit per ten cents a pound, a 10% fall in copper removes about $2.6 billion, and a return to $4.50 removes roughly $8.6 billion - close to half the business. (The deterministic proxy's 24.4% swing per 10% move is computed off the outage-depressed trailing base and therefore overstates the forward sensitivity, which is closer to 13% of normalised earnings; the direction and the danger are the same either way.) Second, cost-curve position. The $1.90-a-pound headline is net of by-product credits struck at $4,000-an-ounce gold and excludes $284 million of idle-facility costs; on a gross basis the company's own 2027 United States target is $2.50 a pound, which it calls challenging. The cohort proxy places Freeport's 34.8% cash operating margin in the highest-cost quartile of eight copper names - roughly half Southern Copper's 63%. A high-cost producer at a record price earns its margin from the price, not from its position, and that margin is the first to go. Third, and decisively, price. Correct for the fact that 36% to 40% of consolidated earnings belong to the Indonesian government, Sumitomo and the Cerro Verde minorities, and at $67.50 the shares already pay roughly nine to ten times the 2027-2028 attributable cash operating profit Freeport itself projects at $6.00-a-pound copper - a fuller multiple than BHP at 8.6 times, Teck at 7.4 or Rio Tinto at 7.2 command on today's trailing numbers at today's strong prices. Our reconciled base-case value is $60 a share; the shares are 12% above it, having risen 6.1% on the day of this review on a record copper print. On capital discipline the verdict is mixed but not damning: distributions of $6.3 billion since 2021, a real 50%-of-excess-cash-flow policy and no top-of-cycle acquisition, set against capital spending stepping from $4.3 billion to $4.8 billion with $1.6 billion of it discretionary, a buyback that bought well at $36.41 in the first half of 2025 and then bought near $64.71 in the June 2026 quarter, and insiders who have sold 632,274 shares and bought none. That is a company drifting toward, but not yet committing, the cycle's classic error. Set against a neutral read on the copper chain, the conclusion is straightforward: wait for the wash-out. The level we want is roughly $50 a share - a 20% margin of safety to the $60 base case - which is where this stock has historically gone whenever copper retraces toward its 200-day average. Below that, the 25-year reserve life, the United States refining franchise and the 2028 volume step are worth owning. At $67.50, with the metal at a record and the adverse case sitting at $33 - a level these shares actually traded at within the last twelve months - the buyer is being paid to take the wrong side of the torque.
